```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false

library(tidyverse)
set.seed(222)
theme_set(theme_bw(22))

# Kelp forest fish biomass at Channel Islands sites. MPAs boost biomass, and
# fished sites recover with distance from port (less fishing pressure).
islands <- c("San Miguel", "Santa Rosa", "Santa Cruz", "Anacapa")
kelp <- tibble(
  island = factor(rep(islands, each = 15), levels = islands),
  protection = factor(
    sample(rep(c("Fished", "MPA"), 30)),
    levels = c("Fished", "MPA")
  ),
  dist_port_km = runif(60, 5, 60)
) |>
  mutate(
    mpa = as.numeric(protection == "MPA"),
    island_effect = c(0, -6, -12, -18)[as.integer(island)],
    biomass = rnorm(
      n(),
      45 + island_effect + 25 * mpa + 0.6 * dist_port_km -
        0.5 * dist_port_km * mpa,
      9
    )
  )

kelp_null <- lm(biomass ~ 1, kelp)
kelp_prot <- lm(biomass ~ protection, kelp)
kelp_island <- lm(biomass ~ island, kelp)
kelp_add <- lm(biomass ~ protection + dist_port_km, kelp)
kelp_int <- lm(biomass ~ protection * dist_port_km, kelp)

# Coral bleaching scenario from Week 4 (Simpson's paradox)
n_per_region <- 40
coral <- tibble(
  region = factor(
    c("Coolest", "Moderate", "Warmest"),
    levels = c("Coolest", "Moderate", "Warmest")
  ),
  sst_mean = c(28, 29, 30),
  region_effect = c(0, -20, -40)
) |>
  slice(rep(1:3, each = n_per_region)) |>
  mutate(
    peak_sst = rnorm(n(), sst_mean, 0.5),
    percent_bleached = -151 + 8 * peak_sst + region_effect + rnorm(n(), 0, 5)
  )
coral_lm <- lm(percent_bleached ~ peak_sst + region, coral)

protection_colours <- c(Fished = "#9ecae1", MPA = "#f4a582")
rss <- function(m) sum(residuals(m)^2)
fmt <- function(x) format(round(x), big.mark = "{,}")

# Fitted model as a LaTeX equation, e.g. biomass = 41.2 + 12.3 MPA + e
eq_tex <- function(m, lhs, labels) {
  b <- coef(m)
  terms <- map2_chr(b[-1], labels, \(x, label) {
    sprintf(
      "%s %.1f \\cdot \\text{%s}",
      if (x < 0) "-" else "+",
      abs(x),
      label
    )
  })
  cat(sprintf(
    "$$\n\\text{%s} = %.1f %s + \\varepsilon\n$$\n",
    lhs,
    b[[1]],
    paste(terms, collapse = " ")
  ))
}

# summary() output without the call, residuals, stars, or R-squared
print_summary <- function(m) {
  out <- capture.output(print(summary(m), signif.stars = FALSE))
  keep <- seq(grep("^Coefficients", out), length(out))
  keep <- setdiff(keep, grep("^Multiple R-squared", out))
  cat(paste0("lm(", deparse(formula(m)), ")"), "", out[keep], sep = "\n")
}

# Points by group (jittered) with each group's fitted value as a horizontal
# segment and residuals drawn as vertical lines
plot_groups <- function(m, group, fill_values = NULL, title = NULL) {
  dat <- kelp |>
    mutate(
      group = {{ group }},
      x = as.integer(group) + runif(n(), -0.2, 0.2),
      fitted = fitted(m)
    )
  fits <- dat |>
    group_by(group) |>
    summarize(fitted = mean(fitted), x = as.integer(first(group)))
  p <- ggplot(dat, aes(x, biomass)) +
    geom_segment(
      aes(xend = x, yend = fitted),
      color = "grey50",
      linewidth = 0.4
    ) +
    geom_segment(
      aes(x = x - 0.35, xend = x + 0.35, y = fitted, yend = fitted),
      fits,
      linewidth = 1.5
    ) +
    geom_point(aes(fill = group), shape = 21, size = 2.5) +
    scale_x_continuous(
      breaks = seq_along(levels(dat$group)),
      labels = str_wrap(levels(dat$group), 6)
    ) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "Fish biomass (g/m²)", title = title) +
    theme(
      legend.position = "none",
      plot.title = element_text(size = 18),
      panel.grid.minor.x = element_blank()
    )
  if (is.null(fill_values)) {
    p + scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2")
  } else {
    p + scale_fill_manual(values = fill_values)
  }
}

# Biomass vs distance from port, with fitted lines per protection status and
# residuals drawn as vertical lines
plot_distance <- function(m, title = NULL) {
  dat <- mutate(kelp, fitted = fitted(m))
  ggplot(dat, aes(dist_port_km, biomass, color = protection)) +
    geom_segment(
      aes(xend = dist_port_km, yend = fitted),
      color = "grey50",
      linewidth = 0.4
    ) +
    geom_line(aes(y = fitted), linewidth = 1.5) +
    geom_point(aes(fill = protection), shape = 21, color = "black", size = 2.5) +
    scale_color_manual(values = protection_colours) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = protection_colours) +
    labs(
      x = "Distance from port (km)",
      y = "Fish biomass (g/m²)",
      color = NULL,
      fill = NULL,
      title = title
    ) +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom", plot.title = element_text(size = 18))
}
```

# Comparing models

## Learning objectives

- **Review** categorical predictors
- **Compute** degrees of freedom from data and model
- **Compare** simpler and more complex models

## This week

More complex models have **benefits**: they explain more variation.

::: {.fragment}

But they have **costs**: they spend more information.

:::

::: {.fragment}

Bonus: some of the most widely used statistical tests (t-test, ANOVA) are _just comparisons_ between linear models of different complexity.

:::

## Our case study

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="55%"}

```{r}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 6
ggplot(kelp, aes(dist_port_km, biomass)) +
  geom_point(aes(fill = protection), shape = 21, size = 3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = protection_colours) +
  labs(
    x = "Distance from port (km)",
    y = "Fish biomass (g/m²)",
    fill = NULL,
    caption = "Simulated data"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

:::

::: {.column style="width:45%; font-size:0.8em;"}

Divers surveyed fish biomass at **60 kelp forest sites** around the Channel Islands.

- `biomass`: fish biomass (g/m²)
- `protection`: Fished or MPA
- `island`: San Miguel, Santa Rosa, Santa Cruz, or Anacapa
- `dist_port_km`: distance from port (km)

:::

:::

# Review categorical predictors

## Dummy variables

Category levels are text. You can't multiply a coefficient by a word!

::: {.fragment}

So we convert categories to **dummy variables**:

- One level becomes the **reference**
- Every other level gets a dummy variable: **1** if the observation is that level, **0** otherwise

:::

::: {.fragment}

$k$ category levels get $k - 1$ dummy variables.

:::

## Dummy variables

```{r}
kelp |>
  slice(c(1, 16, 31, 46, 2, 17)) |>
  transmute(
    island,
    `Santa Rosa` = as.integer(island == "Santa Rosa"),
    `Santa Cruz` = as.integer(island == "Santa Cruz"),
    Anacapa = as.integer(island == "Anacapa")
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lccc")
```

San Miguel is the **reference** level. It doesn't need its own dummy: when all three dummies are 0, it _has_ to be San Miguel.

## 2 categories, represented three ways

::: {style="font-size:0.75em"}

```{r}
#| output: asis
eq_tex(kelp_prot, "biomass", "MPA")
```

:::

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="45%"}

```{r}
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 4.5
plot_groups(kelp_prot, protection, protection_colours)
```

:::

::: {.column width="55%"}

::: {style="font-size:0.75em"}

```{r}
#| class-output: small-output
print_summary(kelp_prot)
```

:::

:::

:::

::: {style="font-size:0.8em"}

$\beta_0$ is the mean of the reference level (Fished). $\beta_1$ is the _difference_ between MPA and Fished.

:::

## 3+ categories, represented three ways

::: {style="font-size:0.75em"}

```{r}
#| output: asis
eq_tex(kelp_island, "biomass", c("SantaRosa", "SantaCruz", "Anacapa"))
```

:::

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="45%"}

```{r}
#| fig-width: 5.5
#| fig-height: 4.5
plot_groups(kelp_island, island)
```

:::

::: {.column width="55%"}

::: {style="font-size:0.75em"}

```{r}
#| class-output: small-output
print_summary(kelp_island)
```

:::

:::

:::

::: {style="font-size:0.8em"}

$\beta_0$ is the mean of the reference level (San Miguel). Each other coefficient is a _difference_ from San Miguel.

:::

# Compute degrees of freedom from data and model

## Degrees of freedom are inference currency

**Data** gives us information. Each observation is one unit.

::: {.fragment}

**Parameters** of a model spend that information. Each coefficient costs one unit.

:::

::: {.fragment}

The difference between the two is our **degrees of freedom**:

$$
df = n - p
$$

$n$ is the number of observations and $p$ is the number of parameters (including the intercept!).

:::

## Information-complexity trade off

More parameters spend df to improve fit.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 14
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-align: center
wiggly <- tibble(x = seq(0, 10, length.out = 20)) |>
  mutate(y = sin(x / 2) * 3 + rnorm(n(), 0, 0.8))
wiggly_grid <- tibble(x = seq(0, 10, length.out = 400))
fit_labels <- c(
  "1" = "Underfit (p = 2, df = 18)",
  "3" = "About right (p = 4, df = 16)",
  "15" = "Overfit (p = 16, df = 4)"
)
wiggly_fits <- map(c(1, 3, 15), \(degree) {
  m <- lm(y ~ poly(x, degree), wiggly)
  mutate(
    wiggly_grid,
    y = predict(m, wiggly_grid),
    fit = fit_labels[[as.character(degree)]]
  )
}) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  mutate(fit = factor(fit, levels = fit_labels))

ggplot(wiggly, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_line(data = wiggly_fits, color = "cornflowerblue", linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_point(shape = 21, fill = "grey70", size = 3) +
  facet_wrap(~fit) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = range(wiggly$y) + c(-1, 1)) +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 18))
```

- **Too few** parameters: model misses real structure (underfitting)
- **Too many** parameters: model fits the noise (overfitting)

::: {.fragment}

Every parameter has to **earn** its df.

:::

## Example: one categorical predictor

::: {style="font-size:0.75em"}

```{r}
#| output: asis
eq_tex(kelp_prot, "biomass", "MPA")
```

:::

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{r}
#| fig-width: 5.5
#| fig-height: 4.5
plot_groups(kelp_prot, protection, protection_colours)
```

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

- $n = `r nrow(kelp)`$ sites
- $p = 2$ parameters ($\beta_0$, $\beta_1$)
- $df = `r nrow(kelp)` - 2 = `r df.residual(kelp_prot)`$

::: {.fragment}

Check `summary()`: _"Residual standard error: `r round(sigma(kelp_prot), 2)` on **`r df.residual(kelp_prot)` degrees of freedom**"_

:::

:::

:::

## Example: add a continuous predictor

::: {style="font-size:0.75em"}

```{r}
#| output: asis
eq_tex(kelp_add, "biomass", c("MPA", "dist"))
```

:::

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{r}
#| fig-width: 5.5
#| fig-height: 4.5
plot_distance(kelp_add)
```

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

- $n = `r nrow(kelp)`$ sites
- $p = 3$ parameters ($\beta_0$, $\beta_1$, $\beta_2$)
- $df = `r nrow(kelp)` - 3 = `r df.residual(kelp_add)`$

::: {.fragment}

We spent **one more** df on distance from port. Was it worth it?

:::

:::

:::

## Which model is better?

```{r}
df_compare <- tibble(
  Model = c("biomass ~ protection", "biomass ~ protection + dist_port_km"),
  p = c(2, 3),
  df = c(df.residual(kelp_prot), df.residual(kelp_add)),
  RSS = c(rss(kelp_prot), rss(kelp_add)),
  `RSS / df` = RSS / df
)
knitr::kable(df_compare, digits = 0, align = "lccrr")
```

::: {.incremental}

- **Benefit**: the residual sum of squares (RSS) dropped by `r round(rss(kelp_prot) - rss(kelp_add))`
- **Cost**: one df
- Leftover noise _per df_ dropped from `r round(rss(kelp_prot) / df.residual(kelp_prot))` to `r round(rss(kelp_add) / df.residual(kelp_add))`. Distance explained more than it cost!

:::

::: {.fragment}

But how much of a drop is _enough_? We need a test statistic.

:::

# Compare simpler and more complex models

## Cost-benefit

Adding a parameter explains more, but at a cost.

::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

**The benefit**

Smaller residuals, more variation explained.

:::

::: {.column}

**The cost**

Spent degrees of freedom. Each parameter has less information behind it.

:::

:::

## Quantify the trade off

$$
F = \frac{(RSS_{simple} - RSS_{complex}) \;/\; (p_{complex} - p_{simple})}{RSS_{complex} \;/\; (n - p_{complex})}
$$

::: {.incremental}

- **Numerator**: improvement in fit _per df spent_
- **Denominator**: leftover noise _per df remaining_
- **Bigger $F$** means the extra parameters were worth it

:::

::: {.fragment}

If the extra parameters are really all 0 (the null hypothesis), $F$ follows an _F distribution_. That gives us a **p-value**.

:::

## Example 1: does protection matter?

```{r}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-align: center
p_null <- plot_groups(
  kelp_null,
  protection,
  protection_colours,
  sprintf("biomass ~ 1 (RSS = %.0f)", rss(kelp_null))
)
p_prot <- plot_groups(
  kelp_prot,
  protection,
  protection_colours,
  sprintf("biomass ~ protection (RSS = %.0f)", rss(kelp_prot))
)
patchwork::wrap_plots(p_null, p_prot)
```

Compare an **intercept-only** model (one mean for every site) to a **two-category** model (one mean per group).

## Example 1: mathematically

```{r}
f_prot <- anova(kelp_null, kelp_prot)
```

$$
F = \frac{(`r fmt(rss(kelp_null))` - `r fmt(rss(kelp_prot))`) \;/\; (2 - 1)}{`r fmt(rss(kelp_prot))` \;/\; (`r nrow(kelp)` - 2)} = `r round(f_prot$F[2], 2)`
$$

::: {style="font-size:0.8em"}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| class-output: small-output
anova(lm(biomass ~ 1, kelp), lm(biomass ~ protection, kelp))
```

:::

::: {.fragment}

Do the two categories explain enough variation to justify the cost? **Yes** (p = `r signif(f_prot[["Pr(>F)"]][2], 2)`).

:::

## Example 1: it's a t-test!

::: {style="font-size:0.8em"}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| class-output: small-output
t.test(biomass ~ protection, kelp, var.equal = TRUE)
```

:::

```{r}
prot_t <- t.test(biomass ~ protection, kelp, var.equal = TRUE)
```

Same p-value. And $t^2 = (`r round(prot_t$statistic, 3)`)^2 = `r round(prot_t$statistic^2, 2)` = F$.

::: {.fragment}

A (two-sample) **t-test** is a comparison between an intercept-only model and a two-category model.

:::

## Example 2: does island matter?

```{r}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-align: center
p_null <- plot_groups(
  kelp_null,
  island,
  title = sprintf("biomass ~ 1 (RSS = %.0f)", rss(kelp_null))
)
p_island <- plot_groups(
  kelp_island,
  island,
  title = sprintf("biomass ~ island (RSS = %.0f)", rss(kelp_island))
)
patchwork::wrap_plots(p_null, p_island)
```

Compare an **intercept-only** model to a **four-category** model. The complex model spends **3** more df.

## Example 2: mathematically

```{r}
f_island <- anova(kelp_null, kelp_island)
```

$$
F = \frac{(`r fmt(rss(kelp_null))` - `r fmt(rss(kelp_island))`) \;/\; (4 - 1)}{`r fmt(rss(kelp_island))` \;/\; (`r nrow(kelp)` - 4)} = `r round(f_island$F[2], 2)`
$$

::: {style="font-size:0.8em"}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| class-output: small-output
anova(lm(biomass ~ 1, kelp), lm(biomass ~ island, kelp))
```

:::

::: {.fragment}

Does island explain enough variation to justify the cost? **Yes** (p = `r signif(f_island[["Pr(>F)"]][2], 2)`).

:::

## Example 2: it's an ANOVA!

::: {style="font-size:0.8em"}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| class-output: small-output
summary(aov(biomass ~ island, kelp))
```

:::

Same F, same p-value.

::: {.fragment}

A (one-way) **ANOVA** is a comparison between an intercept-only model and a model with a 3+ category predictor.

:::

::: {.fragment}

ANOVA asks: is _at least one_ group mean different? Not _which_ one.

:::

## Example 3: does the slope vary?

```{r}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 5.5
#| fig-align: center
p_add <- plot_distance(
  kelp_add,
  sprintf("Additive (RSS = %.0f)", rss(kelp_add))
)
p_int <- plot_distance(
  kelp_int,
  sprintf("Interactive (RSS = %.0f)", rss(kelp_int))
)
patchwork::wrap_plots(p_add, p_int, guides = "collect") &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Compare an **additive** model (parallel lines) to an **interactive** model (slopes vary). The complex model spends **1** more df.

## Example 3: mathematically

```{r}
f_int <- anova(kelp_add, kelp_int)
```

$$
F = \frac{(`r fmt(rss(kelp_add))` - `r fmt(rss(kelp_int))`) \;/\; (4 - 3)}{`r fmt(rss(kelp_int))` \;/\; (`r nrow(kelp)` - 4)} = `r round(f_int$F[2], 2)`
$$

::: {style="font-size:0.8em"}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| class-output: small-output
anova(
  lm(biomass ~ protection + dist_port_km, kelp),
  lm(biomass ~ protection * dist_port_km, kelp)
)
```

:::

::: {.fragment}

Does the interaction explain enough variation to justify the cost? **Yes** (p = `r signif(f_int[["Pr(>F)"]][2], 2)`).

:::

## Example 3: look familiar?

When the models differ by **one** parameter, the F-test matches the t-test on that coefficient in `summary()`.

::: {style="font-size:0.8em"}

```{r}
#| class-output: small-output
coef(summary(kelp_int))
```

:::

```{r}
int_t <- coef(summary(kelp_int))["protectionMPA:dist_port_km", "t value"]
```

$t^2 = (`r round(int_t, 3)`)^2 = `r round(int_t^2, 2)` = F$

::: {.fragment}

The F-test generalizes: it can test **many** parameters at once.

:::

# Recap

## Recap

::: {.incremental}

- More data means more **information** to spend on inference
- What do we spend it on? **Parameters.** $df = n - p$
- More complex models explain more variation, but do they explain _enough_ variation to justify their costs?
- The **F-test** compares the improvement per df spent to the leftover noise per df remaining
- **t-tests** and **ANOVAs** are F-tests between an intercept-only model and a categorical model

:::
